A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PIE research and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original experiments and Appendix A.1 can be matched reliably to their retained content in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original RepoBench experiments measuring prediction accuracy and cache-update latency, together with representation-similarity and prediction-divergence analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds CodeLlama evaluations, HumanEval/HumanEval-X generation results, and experiments with contextually related edits.

M1.justification: Both versions encode new tokens, correct subsequent cached keys' rotary positions, and reuse subsequent values through the same Equations (1)–(9). The added CodeLlama experiments apply the existing PIE procedure.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates repository-level next-line completion in Python and Java under random insertion, deletion, and mixed multi-place edits. v2 adds HumanEval Python and HumanEval-X C++ code generation, plus target-related insertion and multi-place insertion scenarios. These substantially broaden task, language, and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: Full-recomputation and Conflict Fast Encoding remain the original comparators, including in the new CodeLlama experiments. Tables 8–10 additionally evaluate a Reuse baseline that leaves the pre-edit context unchanged.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings remain unchanged. Added protocols introduce CodeLlama 7B/34B configurations, three-consecutive-line prompt insertions evaluated with Pass@1, and edit-distance-selected RepoBench edits involving 5, 7, 11, 13, or 15 lines. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained edited-token, representation-similarity, and KL-divergence analyses, Appendices B.2–B.3 test robustness to target-related and multi-place insertions across edit sizes. These directly examine more consequential edits than the original random-edit construction, with additional reuse controls.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments are repeated three times with different seeds and averaged scores are reported. v2 adds no distinct uncertainty-reporting practice, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results; added trailing zeros are formatting changes. Tables 5–10 add substantial results for CodeLlama, generation, and related-edit robustness. For example, Table 8 reports PIE Pass@1 of 43.9/49.7 for Python/C++, versus 49.4/50.3 for full recomputation and 17.7/29.2 for reuse. These are new evaluations, not improvements to the original same-setting scores.

T1.justification: The explicit edited-sequence definition and inserted-token list in v1 Section 3.1 are replaced by the literal placeholder 'todo' in v2. This removes a formal specification, although the rotary-position derivation and Equations (1)–(9) remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same PIE contribution and claims of substantial cache-update savings while approximating or preserving full-recomputation accuracy. The added appendix evidence does not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix B.1 newly explains that three-line edits in HumanEval's roughly 15-line prompts are semantically significant and interprets the reuse baseline's weakness as evidence that cache updates matter. B.2–B.3 extend the robustness interpretation to related edits; the original temporal-confusion explanation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents code availability through a repository link in the abstract. Existing implementation disclosures, including Transformers, greedy generation of 64 tokens, batch size one, and A100 hardware arrangements, are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for CodeLlama, HumanEval, and CodeGeeX/HumanEval-X to support the expanded experiments. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to positional encodings and inference-efficiency methods remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 adds appendix subsections and acknowledgements, updates affiliations and publication headers, and makes limited grammar and cross-reference edits. Section 3.1 also acquires an unfinished 'todo' sentence.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the empirical displays: three CodeLlama comparison tables, a Pass@1 table, and two tables organized by edit size. Existing figures retain their designs, while original tables and surrounding text are redistributed across pages.

improvement.justification: v1's reliance on random RepoBench edits and one model family is substantially addressed by CodeLlama validation, generation-level Pass@1 evaluation, and related-edit robustness tests with a reuse control in Appendices A.2 and B. These additions make the method's usefulness and accuracy costs much better supported. That gain outweighs the localized loss of the sequence definition to 'todo', although the retained unqualified accuracy-preservation wording still needs qualification.
